utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the proceedings will continue. Please have the witness brought in, please. (The accused/witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good morning to the interpreters. Good morning to counsel, Defence and Prosecution, Mr. Nobilo, Mr. Hayman. Good morning to the witness, General Blaskic. Everybody is ready? General Blaskic, are you ready?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I'm ready. Thank you. If I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe. Yes, did you want to say something? Mr. Kehoe, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President and Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, you told us that you received the report from -- I'm referring to the truck bomb incident. You received the report from SIS sometime in May that the Vitezovi were involved in the truck bomb incident and that you called Darko Kraljevic in to take disciplinary actions. Now, General, did you also tell him to immediately arrest those in the Vitezovi that were involved in this incident and turn their names over to the military police for prosecution?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I asked him to undertake measures vis-à-vis the perpetrators linked to the incident and that terrorist act, and I also told him to convey his knowledge to the competent authorities and to tell me what had been done. If I may, Mr. President, I made a mistake yesterday in answering the Prosecutor with regard to the mistreatment of Bosniak Muslims temporarily detained in the cinema. I made a mistake with regard to the name of the individual who was mistreated. The individual's name was Suad Salkic, and he was mistreated by a member of the HVO, Mr. Marko from the village of Zabilje, and measures were taken against him. The mistreatment of Hasan Gerdijanovic was outside the cinema. I assume it took place at the checkpoint, in relation to the Bosniak Muslims that I mentioned yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification, General Blaskic, but I think after that we had decided that was not the correct date; is that correct? Prosecutor -- what you're talking about is an incident that had taken place subsequently but thank you for the clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, with regard to the Vitezovi, did you demand that they arrest, or that members in the Vitezovi be arrested, and that warrants be delivered to the military police as soon as possible?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said that I requested the commander of the Vitezovi to take steps vis-à-vis the perpetrators. First of all, I had in mind measures to identify the perpetrators, because in all the investigations the greatest problem was to arrive at the names of the perpetrators. That was the biggest problem in the circumstances that existed during that time frame while there was ongoing fighting. It was the most difficult thing to arrive at names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, let me show you your orders at defendant's 360 and 361. Now, General, defendant's 360 and 361 are two orders that you issued. Defendant's 360 is an order that you issued on the 23rd of April, 1993 to all subordinate commanders, and it discusses the behaviour of HVO members and the level of military discipline. On number 4 of this order, you forbid all HVO units to carry out offensive actions, and this order is to come into effect immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me. Could we put the ELMO on, please? The ELMO's not on. It's on over there. The monitor we have is off, Mr. President, but we can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In 361, General, which is an order of yours dated the 28th of April, 1993 to commanders of all units of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, and you're discussing elimination of arbitrary acts by commanders and individuals, you order: "After an assessment carried out on in the field, it is apparent that the lower commanders and the units are acting outside of the chain of command." In number 3 of this order you order: "The individuals and groups who are completely out of control are to be arrested immediately and warrants are to be delivered to the commander of the Military Police unit." Now, these two orders, General, apply to the Vitezovi and Darko Kraljevic, do they not?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Document 361, in the title says: "To the Commanders of all the units in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone," that is, to stop arbitrary acts by commanders and individuals. It is a document addressed to all the commanders. Document 360 applies to all subordinate commanders of the HVO, that is to say, within the structure of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, the question is: These orders apply to Kraljevic's unit, the Vitezovi, as well, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Order 361 applies to Kraljevic as well, I'm certain of that. Order 360, as it was written at the time, I'm not quite sure whether it was sent to that unit because it refers to the subordinate units within the HVO, that is to say, the units within the structure. This particular order, that is to say, 361, in point 1 appears to be absurd because I ordered that an order be carried out. So it is an order to an order, and it focuses on an attempt to introduce law and order, which can be seen from point 4 and 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, General. The question is whether or not it applies to Kraljevic and the Vitezovi. That was the question.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I've answered that. Document 361, I'm quite certain, refers to that because it is addressed to the commanders of all the units, that is. Whereas document 360, I'm not quite sure whether it refers to that because it mentions all subordinate officers of the HVO, that is to say, within the Central Bosnia Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In response to a question by Judge Shahabuddeen when you discussed these two exhibits, you noted, in talking about Kraljevic: "A I made him aware of that through my order D360 and 361 and precisely to avoid this sort of self-will, Your Honour. I sent it to him as well, which meant that it referred to his unit as well." This is on page 19506, lines 12 through 15. So you told Judge Shahabuddeen that these two orders refer to Kraljevic's unit, the Vitezovi, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I said that document 361, from the title, and it is about the elimination and suppression of arbitrariness of commanders and individuals, but it refers to all the units within the Central Bosnia Operative Zone. Document 360, linked to the heading, I'm not sure whether it was sent to the Vitezovi as well, because it refers to units within the structure of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, but at all events, there was arbitrariness of conduct of units not within the structure. There was self-will and arbitrariness on the part of groups including the Vitezovi and the commander of the Vitezovi. So there was arbitrary action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, General, when you told Judge Shahabuddeen that 360 and 361 applied to the Vitezovi, are you saying you're mistaken, or you didn't know what you were talking about, or you left something out? I mean, what's your answer?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: My answer is that I'm absolutely certain that document 361, which speaks about the suppression of self-will on the part of commanders and individuals included all the units in the Operative Zone, that is to say, I wanted to remind them of their duties, whereas document 360, I said I'm not fully certain whether it included units which were only added to the Vitezovi and the military police. Perhaps it does, because from the title, I'm looking at the head and it says, "To all subordinate commanders," but in essence, the documents are similar. Both documents are similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, let us talk about your order in 361. Did you demand that Kraljevic identify and arrest members of the Vitezovi that were responsible for this heinous crime involved with the truck bomb? Did you do that? And do you have a written order to support that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can we keep the question simple and not compound, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The question is very simple. If he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, I have to acknowledge, Mr. Hayman, that frequently the questions are simple and the answers are complicated. Let me also remind you that you don't have any specific role to play here because the witness is alone. The answers are frequently simple and the answers are frequently complicated. Please don't forget that we have noted a change of answers in respect of an answer that was asked by one of my colleagues in the Trial Chamber. Therefore, Mr. Kehoe, please continue, because I could also ask the question, Mr. Hayman, how is it that on the 23rd of April General Blaskic addressed an order to commanders except to Darko Kraljevic on the 23rd of April, as I said, whereas, in fact, it was a unit that acted in a particularly illegal way, that in any way -- we frequently ask very direct questions and that's what we'll do. Let's not waste any time. Mr. Kehoe, please continue. I ask General Blaskic to try to answer directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you hear my question, General, or would you like me to repeat it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please repeat the question so that the witness is sure to understand it. Thank you, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, did you demand that Darko Kraljevic arrest individuals in the Vitezovi who were responsible for this truck bomb crime?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. That seems to me to be a simple question.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I demanded that he conduct an investigation as to the truck bomb explosion, and this implied that he would send in the names of the perpetrators, take them into custody or send the list to the military police for the military police to do so. But I demanded that he conduct an investigation until he had identified the perpetrators by name and surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, to your knowledge, was anyone arrested for this crime ever?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I know, nobody -- I say, as far as I know, nobody was arrested because the names and surnames of the perpetrators were never uncovered, the perpetrators of the crime, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I take it that nobody was ever disciplined and removed from the HVO for committing this crime as well?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as my data and information goes, the investigation did not result in uncovering the perpetrators of the crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, how about during your sweeping investigation known as Operation Pauk? Did your sweeping investigation of war crimes launch an investigation into this heinous acts to uncover the names of the members of the Vitezovi who committed this act?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Operation Pauk implied an investigation of all crimes committed in the area of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, this crime took place 400 metres from your headquarters in April of 1993. While you were running Operation Pauk, did you conduct an investigation of this terrible crime that your chief of staff called a terrorist act?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have already stated that Operation Pauk was an operation of all crimes. It is true that this was 400 metres away, but it is also true that it was the other side of the front line which was inaccessible to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: General Blaskic, I say this for Mr. Hayman, this is typically the kind of answer that doesn't match the question asked. I'm sorry, Mr. Hayman, but now there are some questions being asked twice. As part of Operation Spider, was there an investigation ordered while the witness was in a position to do so, that is, about the truck bomb? The answer is always reminding us of what Operation Spider was about. We know what it was about. Please answer the question. The question asked was: As part of Operation Spider, did you carry out an investigation or try to collect information about the truck bomb? The question is a very simple one; "Yes," "No," or something else?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The investigation of Operation Pauk included all crimes committed, including the truck bomb, and all the crimes committed in the area of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. This is the third time that you're saying about the truck bomb. That's what you've just said.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know what the interpretation was that reached you, but the investigation under Operation Pauk which included war crimes included all crimes committed, that is to say, including the crime committed by the truck bomb explosion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Among other things, that's what you've said. All right. That's the answer. Now we have an answer. Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In your investigation of the truck bomb in Operation Pauk, was anybody ever arrested for their involvement in the truck bomb incident in Stari Vitez; "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, because, as I've already stated, a list, a file of the investigation did not result in names, except the Vitezovi unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So the investigation by SIS in May didn't result in any names and your investigation in Operation Pauk in 1994 also didn't result in any names; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have already stated that the investigation within Operation Pauk was an investigation of all crimes, including that particular crime, and it did not result in any names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: As a result of this terrorist act, if we can conclude from your Operation Pauk, nobody was arrested, nobody was convicted, and no soldier was ever disciplined for this heinous act? That's the bottom line, isn't it, General?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is the bottom line, but I'd just like to add that the results of the investigation did not result in identifying the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, did your chief of staff, Slavko Marin, know that you had launched SIS into an investigation of the truck bomb in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't believe that at that particular moment he knew, perhaps later, because the orders which went towards the SIS assistant were something that Slavko Marin need not have been aware of. So I don't know whether he knew or not. Quite possibly he did, but the order was, at all events, certainly sent to the assistant for SIS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me read you two versions of his testimony at page 13433, line 4: "Q Brigadier, was there any order sent out by Colonel Blaskic to ask anyone whether HVO soldiers, any HVO soldiers, were responsible for this explosion? A I do not know whether an order of that kind was sent out." On the same page, line 17, referring to the report from the Vitez Brigade: "Q So this report that we see, Defence Exhibit 304, after Blaskic received this report from the Vitez Brigade, he was satisfied that he had all information about the bomb and took no further steps that you know of to find out who was responsible; is that right? A I do not know what the commander was aware of and what was undertaken following that report." So, General, it appears clear that your chief of operations and then your acting chief of staff was unaware of any investigation that you asked for with respect to this truck bomb incident?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He was the chief of operations, Slavko Marin, that we're talking about, and he was in charge of combat activities specifically, whereas the SIS security is a secret security working on its own assignments. As far as I was able to understand, he says that he was not aware of it, but I did issue an assignment and required an investigation from the security assistant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you have a written order that supports what you just said?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have been listening to this for at least the fifth time in the last two days, whether there was a written order. First of all, the witness has answered. Second, it is not up to him to prove anything. Does the Prosecutor have evidence that he did not do that? Because the situation seems to be turning around. The same questions are being posed and, in a way, the witness is being maltreated, badgered, with the same questions, and then it would appear as if the witness is not answering correctly, has to repeat his answers. But this is all an artificial product to gain an effect which I don't think is the correct way to conduct a examination. This question was answered at least five times, that it was an oral order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I'll give you an answer, Mr. Nobilo. I believe that in all legal systems, the Prosecutor has to prove what he's putting forth. From that point of view, I render tribute to you, and you're right. But in all legal systems throughout the world, when the Prosecutor puts forth information which has to do with a witness, in this example a witness, not an accused, a witness who is giving answers by saying, "I did this" or "I did that," in all legal systems, the one who is putting forth the information has to at least begin to provide some evidence for what he's saying. Do you agree with what I've said on that point?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, but I don't agree that every two hours the same thing should be asked and to create the conviction that there is no proof for that assertion, that is to say, I am against having the same question repeated again and again. These are effects to play to a jury but not to this type of Tribunal, with professional judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We are not talking about juries here. As you stated have correctly, we are professional judges and we know, when the time comes, how to sift through what is solid evidence and what is an allegation made by the Prosecutor. I'm merely saying to you that this is not a witness like other witnesses but rather an accused who issued many orders and about whom one could think that he had issued orders that were issued in order to support his thesis. You are not the one who cannot show me that I'm wrong on that point, and perhaps that's a natural thing. The witness, who is also an accused, has issued orders, and having issued the orders, Mr. Nobilo, he places himself into a situation in which the Judges have all of the orders issued. Are you following me in the way I'm reasoning? I'm speaking slowly and I'm asking the interpreters to be very careful about what I'm saying. This is not a witness like other witnesses. This is a witness who is also an accused and who, in his own defence and with your competent assistance, produced a number of orders. This is my first way of reasoning. When he tried to establish his defence in respect of the production of orders, it is absolutely natural for the opposing party or even for the Judges to put themselves in the same perspective, that is, the perspective of the orders that he issued. That's the second part of my reasoning. My third reason is the fact that the witness himself is the one who said, "I gave an order to do this," or "I gave an order to do that." Therefore, it doesn't seem illegitimate for the Prosecutor to say, "Do you have an order?" Now, if he doesn't have it, Mr. Nobilo, that's not a reason for the Judges to draw the most negative consequences that you could imagine. The trial has been going on for two years and many things have been said. But when we speak about methodology, it does not seem illegitimate to me for the opposing party, in this case, the Prosecutor, when the witness says, "I gave an order to do this or that," for the Prosecutor to ask, "Do you have the order or don't you?" If he doesn't, he doesn't. That's all there is. Do you agree with the way I'm reasoning, Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Almost fully, Your Honour. I almost fully agree with the logical sequence that you have just presented. However, there are two premises that you omitted to mention. One is that the witness said that he issued an oral order. He said that at least a few times yesterday. So if he issued an oral order, that means that he could not have the order in writing. That is one thing. The second thing is that I do not agree with the same question being repeated five or six times in two days, and he has answered. But I do agree with your logic. Look at another effect. The witness said that he gave an oral order to Kraljevic in May, and a few minutes ago, the Prosecutor asked him, in Defence Exhibit 366 from the 24th of April, 1993, he said, "Where's your order to carry out an investigation related to the truck bomb?" Well, he could have taken any other order and asked where it was because it's not there. He issued the order orally in May. I'm objecting to this because all of this is actually badgering the witness, and the witness has to answer the same questions five times, and key questions at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, thank you for your contribution to this discussion. But it is very important for the Judges, and the Prosecutor's questions are important for the Judges, it could be very important for the Judges, for example, to note that the important orders which might come to support what the witness is saying were always oral orders. Do you see what I mean? What is important, in fact, is oral. You, through the witness, produced written orders which do not always have a numerical sequence. Do you remember we had this discussion about the numbers? For the Judges, therefore, it could be important for the proceedings to note that many orders are missing and that when the witness tells us that he gave an order to carry out an investigation, we note that it was an oral order. If this occurs frequently, that is, that there are frequently oral orders, that it might be important for the Judges to note that very frequently very important orders about very important subjects were given orally. All we will do is take note of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: May it please the Court? I just have one more sentence, and I thank you for having opened this debate. It is important to understand military conduct. Never, absolutely never, does a commander in any army issue command orders in writing to his immediate associates, the members of his command. Written orders are given to units outside headquarters, but at morning briefings issues are given orally to members of his command. So that is to say that all orders to Ivica Zejko, to the intelligence service, Nakic, all of them are oral, and they would be oral in any army in the world. If there is an order in writing, then that is dramatic and that is why there are these two written orders. You will never find them in any headquarters in any army in the world that the members of one's immediate command get orders in writing. These are people who sit in an operations room together. Their desks are right next to one another. They would not write to one another to give orders to each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: First of all, I would answer by saying that these crimes are not daily occurrences, the most serious crimes. In the second place, your witness said how upset he was by the crimes. He said that. He repeated that. It appears -- remember that he gave orders, orders that you were very pleased to show to the Judges, written orders about Ahmici and orders about the military offences including the truck bomb. In the second place, your witness held important responsibilities during Operation Spider. He was very satisfied -- very pleased to say that to the Judges. Mr. Nobilo, one cannot be satisfied with presenting certain facts to the Judges and then to protest when the opposing party or the Judges ask for additions to those facts. It's like the alibi defence, which you did not use, but in all legal systems throughout the world, when a witness says something, and here this is a witness, he does so under his own responsibility, and his responsibility includes, even if he might one day -- if he might even say, "Where is the order?" The Judges have to point out and take note of the fact that many of the orders issued were oral, and frequently the orders that your witness wants to show as support of his statements are not there and this is an important thing for the Judges to know. That is what I wanted to say to you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, before we move away from this area, I would like to read you one more short excerpt of testimony of Lieutenant-Colonel Henk Morsink at page 9858, at line 15: "Q In respect to the truck bomb that occurred in Stari Vitez, when Mario Cerkez said he was going to conduct an investigation, when you were in theatre did you ever receive an investigative report from the HVO about the circumstances of that truck bomb?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Never." So, General, was the international community made aware of the results of this alleged investigation you launched as to who was responsible for the truck bomb?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: First of all, the investigation was not an alleged investigation, it really was carried out, so I have to repeat once again that the report that I received from the security service said that the Vitezovi unit was behind this. This was not an alleged investigation, this was an investigation that was truly carried out. Secondly, I never had an approval -- I never had approval to acquaint the members of the International Community with the results of the investigation, and members of the international organisations were not entitled to receive this kind of information, because I had the law on military secrets that I had to operate in accordance with. So I had to keep these secrets, and these internal difficulties and problems I usually -- nobody usually shared with members of the International Community.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, let us move ahead and stay with the Vitezovi. We will move ahead chronologically to the attack on Stari Vitez of the 18th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Just before you change gears, may I can take the opportunity of asking General Blaskic whether Exhibits 360 and 361 also applied to the military police? You know, General, we've been talking about the Vitezovi and about SIS. I want to be clear about the situation of the military police.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honour, document 361 certainly pertains to the military police too. Yes, it does. But document 360, as I've already said, speaks about all the subordinate commanders within the Operative Zone. Perhaps it was supposed to be a reminder to the military police too. Perhaps it pertained to them as well, but I'm not 100 per cent sure. However, as far as 361 is concerned, that I'm sure about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So at that point of time, you were taking the view that the military police were subordinate to you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The military police was not subordinated to me in that period of time. It was attached to me. It was subordinated to me only from the end of July, the beginning of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, you spoke about introducing or reintroducing the rule of law. Should I take it that, therefore, you felt the need for the assistance of the military police to help you in that endeavour?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, certainly, Your Honour, because the military police or, rather, one the tasks of the military police is to discover the perpetrators of crimes, making files about the perpetrators of crimes and sending these files to the district military prosecutor on the basis of the law on criminal procedure, and I think the witness Tadic spoke about that here too now. However, when the military police is not directly subordinated to me in terms of my direct command, then it is not one of my direct instruments in this regard and, therefore, I'm brought into an absurd situation. In document 360, in item number 1, I ask that the previously issued order be carried out. I am absurdly repeating that my order should be carried out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I see. Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Shahabuddeen. All right. You want to now speak about the Vitezovi, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, among other things we are going to talk about the attack on Stari Vitez on the 18th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, you told us that on the morning of the 18th of July, 1993, I think you told us you weren't in Vitez. Can you just tell us what you did that morning, once again?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 18th I was in Busovaca. I attended mass in the church there, and I was with the priest from Busovaca. I had lunch at his place that afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, General, just to clarify, did you go from the Hotel Vitez to mass in Busovaca, attend mass and then have lunch with the local parish priest?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I left my headquarters. I think it was in Nova Bila. Yes, I left Nova Bila on the evening of the 17th. I went to Busovaca, to a place called Ravan. I spent the night there with Petrovic family, the family of Ivo Petrovic. They are my close relatives. In the morning I attended holy mass and I had lunch in Busovaca, in the town of Busovaca, at the parish priest's home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What time did this attack commence in Stara Bila [real-time error] on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I will have to look this up in my chronology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. Check what you need to check. Were you able to find your chronology, Mr. Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, not yet, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The time of the attack on Stara Bila, I think that's what was translated here. You're talking about Stara Bila?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Stari Vitez. It should be Stari Vitez. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: This shouldn't be too complicated, General Blaskic. The Prosecutor is giving you a specific date. You know, you gave all the information minute by minute and it's in your chronology. We're speaking about the 18th; is that correct, the 18th of July, 1993. At what time, Mr. Kehoe? Is this information that the witness himself gave?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm not positive he actually gave it, Mr. President. He gave us an account of what happened that day and his movements between Nova Bila and in Busovaca, I believe, and the simple question I had was: What time did this action begin in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It was an operation that was carried out by the HVO commander. I don't remember. Could you refresh our memory, please while the General is looking through his chronology.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That was an operation carried out by the HVO in Stari Vitez on the 18th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, why don't you look at that at the break and we'll move on with the questioning. General, my next question -- if you can put that down and we can move on to the break and you can look at that on the break. When did you find out, what time of day did you find out that there had been an attack on Stari Vitez, do you recall? I'll remind you of your testimony that you said at page 19496, that you returned to Nova Bila at 18.00.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: When I came back to Nova Bila, that is to say, that afternoon, I found out that there had been combat activity in Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You had no information about that combat activity until you returned to your headquarters at Nova Bila at 18.00; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not have any such information or knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thereafter, did you learn any of the methods employed during that attack, such as the use of "babies" to be launched into Stari Vitez. That being, of course, fire extinguishers being filled with various types of munitions.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were such stories too, possibly, but I found out that the following method was used: To use the fog for attracting BH army units into Stara Bila and thus contributing to the surprise factor. That's what the commanders talked about most of all. However, this was an entire story saying that this was a major victory of the BH army and there were major losses on the HVO side and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. I think you've answered the question. Please continue, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But you realised -- you do know, as a military commander, that the use of "babies," the launching of these fire extinguishers, launches a projectile which can't be controlled; isn't that right? Certainly the direction can't be controlled.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It wasn't the way you are saying. It wasn't only that. These were explosives, not only fire extinguishers, and they were used at short range, and usually at BH army positions. There were stories, stories, rumours that "babies" were used too, but I know that the artillery of the Operative Zone was not used and that nobody asked me to have the artillery used.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The use of these "babies" is illegal under the laws of war; isn't it, because they are fired and land indiscriminately; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: This is your assertion, Mr. Kehoe. Please ask your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Are the use of these "babies," which are fire extinguishers stuffed with munitions, are the use of those illegal in that they land indiscriminately?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, our client is not a lawyer. It calls for a legal conclusion. That's a question for the Court, not the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: During your training --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I sustained the objection. Don't ask legal questions unless they are questions about something that a commander should really know, but I agree with Mr. Hayman. Remember that the witness said that as a military commander, he knew what was lawful and what was not lawful, but it is true, Mr. Kehoe, try not to draw the witness into legal discussions that are too complicated. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, these "babies," were they precise? By "precise," I'm talking about can you specifically direct their direction and where they are about to land when they explode?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as directing them in a certain direction, that was possible. As far as I know, this was done by members of the BH army in the territory of Zabilje or the positions of Brdo, Stozerak. They were used at 150-metre, 200-metre ranges, and they were precise to a certain extent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. Try to answer from a technical point of view. It's not a legal issue. The question was whether these weapons were precise and whether they could be controlled, that is, relatively possible to control them and be precise. Answer the question, please.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Weapons can relatively be controlled, and they are precise but they are used at shorter ranges, 150 to 200 metres. The few crews that are trained for that can hit a military target with that. Yes, it can be directed and controlled because military rules imply the use of mortars without using sight devices, with other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, based on your training as a military commander, would you consider the use of these "babies" a proper use in war or an improper use?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The situation that we were in then was such that we simply did not have any other choice or any other way out, but we certainly tried to reduce this kind of use to a minimum and to keep everything under control. There were many difficulties in this situation of chaos. It would have been better had there been no need to wage war in such an area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, General, during your time as the commander in the Central Bosnian Operative Zone, did you authorise the use of these "babies" in combat?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not remember having authorised the use of "babies" in combat, but I know that there was such use. I had received all kinds of information or rumours. There were improvised means that were used from rifles to artillery guns practically. That's what people did in the situation of self-defence. The greatest difficulty was to keep all of this under control, that is to say, to register all these weapons and keep them under control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, let us move back to the Stari Vitez attack on the 18th where you told us you received no information about that attack until 18.00 when you returned to your headquarters. I'd like to show you a photograph, Prosecutor's Exhibit 433/4. General, who is the man to the left-hand side of that photograph?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is Darko Gelic, an officer in charge of relations with UNPROFOR. He was an administrative officer in the command of the Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me read to you some descriptions that have been given by some witnesses about Darko Gelic, General. First, by Captain Lee Whitworth who noted that, and this is a series of pages, at transcript page 10193, 10195, 10198, 10217, 10296, 10298, Whitworth described Gelic as: "A ... Blaskic's liaison officer and did the speaking for then Colonel Blaskic during this period of time. A good number of meetings were with Gelic rather than Blaskic." At page 10341, Whitworth said he would petition Blaskic, usually through Gelic, to make stuff happen. On page 10414, on one occasion when Whitworth went to meet with Blaskic but met with Gelic instead, Whitworth on page 10433 noted that he assumed that the Blaskic/Gelic relationship was the same as the Whitworth/Duncan relationship and that he was acting on behalf of the Colonel, that is, with his authority and blessing. Major Mark Bower noted about the relationship with Gelic at page 9425 that Major Bower dealt with Gelic at the Hotel Vitez when he needed access through checkpoints. At page 9427, Bower spoke to Gelic to gain access to Kruscica for a food convoy. On page 9459, Bower noted that getting convoys through generally was facilitated through Gelic. On page 9493, Bower noted that if he wanted to evacuate casualties from Stari Vitez, he would invariably have to go to Hotel Vitez and speak with Gelic. Brigadier Alastair Duncan, at 9164, described Darko Gelic as the HVO Operative Zone Central Bosnia Liaison Officer to BritBat, and the same, Lieutenant Colonel Morsink identified Darko Gelic as Blaskic's liaison officer, and that was at page 9935 and 9940. General, Darko Gelic was the person who you authorised to speak to the international representatives and especially to BritBat during a period of time when he was your liaison officer in Central Bosnia; is that accurate, sir?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is not correct that he was the officer who could talk to international representatives, regardless of which international representatives we're talking about, because the question is what would he talk about? He was an officer who could receive information from liaison officers of the international representatives, and then he could communicate this information to me or to other persons in charge to which this information was addressed, or he could also convey our positions to the UNPROFOR officers or other persons to whom this information was addressed to. So he was the officer who was in charge of conveying this information. He did not have any other powers, only administration, that is to say, to receive information and convey information related to meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think you've answered. The person who both receives and transmits seems a lot for a transmission officer. That's a subtle nuance, but I thought that I understood that he received things and that he was authorised to transmit things and then to let people know what you had said. I'm not asking a question. I'm just making a comment. Please continue, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us move to a document, General, if we may.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Prosecution Exhibit 708.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this is a military information summary of the British Battalion dated the 18th of July, 1993. The designation on the top is "1 PWO Milinfosum," that is the abbreviated description of 1 Prince of Wales Own Regiment of Yorkshire, who was, of course, the successor British battalion after the Cheshire Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I would like to refer to the first two paragraphs, the "General Situation" and "Vitez," and I will read it slowly for you, General, as it's in English. Again, this is dated 18 July, 1993: "In the Lasva Valley, the HVO have launched an attack on the Muslim pocket of Stari Vitez ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you pull that down, please, Mr. Usher? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "... The outcome is presently unknown as fighting is ongoing and access into the area is being denied. An HVO attack on the Vrbas valley has not yet materialised but there are signs of mounting tension ..." If we could move to Vitez. "2. BritBat echelon report that Vitez had its busiest night since the arrival of 1 PWO. A human intelligence source claimed last night that the HVO were about to attack Stari Vitez," and it gives a grid reference. "During the night there was the normal small arms and HMG fire punctuated by mortar fire but on the 18th at 04.45 an intensive barrage of the Muslim area began and involved occasional MBRL and artillery fire as well as mortars. The fighting has continued throughout the day. 3 Corps BiH have stated that there were 15 casualties in Stari Vitez but it is unclear whether this is a total figure or merely those requiring evacuation. Pero Skopljak, HDZ mayor of Vitez, has also spoken to ops concerning the evacuation of wounded. All access into Vitez has been denied by HVO checkpoints located at," two grid references, "225935 and at grid 243923. Both checkpoints have mines laid across the road and troops with cam cream were noted in the area of the first checkpoint. Darko Gelic, the Operative Zone Central Bosnia liaison officer to BritBat, has confirmed that the HVO are attacking Stari Vitez and that the artillery barrage was the preliminary phase. At 181459, echelon reported that the Croat village of Veceriska was coming under small arms, HMG and mortar fire. Similarly, at 182031 mortar fire was reported on the Croat village of Jardol. At the time of the writing the fighting is ongoing. Comment. The HVO have frequently in the past threatened action against Stari Vitez. That they are apparently actioning this threat now is testimony to their current confidence in their position. Whether this confidence is justified remains to be seen as the BiH are undoubtedly in the stronger position throughout the area. The HVO may be merely exploiting the fact that 3 Corps' attention is apparently elsewhere. Comment ends." In portion 3: "3. Darko Gelic also confirmed the helicopter flight into the Vitez area reported yesterday and stated that it was bringing in 'some piece of very important equipment.' He also claimed that the helicopter had 2 pilots, one for day and one for night." Now, General, here is your liaison officer discussing this barrage or this attack with a liaison officer in the British Battalion, and he notes that the artillery fire, the artillery barrage was the preliminary phase of the attack. Was this man speaking on your behalf, sir?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: First of all, he's commenting on the activity on Stari Vitez. He was a liaison officer, but I'd like to underline that the HVO did not launch an attack on Stari Vitez but this was done by the members of the PPN Vitezovi, special purposes. According to my chronology, on the 17th of July, the night before, there was artillery fire on the part of the BH army in the centre of Vitez and other areas of Vitez. The artillery that I commanded did not fire at Stari Vitez at any time, and the result of the attack on the 18th of July by the Vitezovi was general condemnation sent to me because it was claimed that I had not allowed the artillery of the HVO to fire on Stari Vitez. Nobody even asked me or informed me about that attack and those activities. Darko Gelic comments on the arrival of helicopters. According to my notes, we arrived only at the beginning of August 1993 and not in July 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, this military information summary notes that the artillery barrage began at 04.45 in the morning. Is it your testimony that between 04.45 in the morning and 18.00 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The interpreters are not following. I am now at the end of General Blaskic's answer. All right. What's your question? I can read it, but I want to be sure that the witness has time to answer the question. Please continue, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This military information summary reflects that the artillery attack on Stari Vitez began at 4.45 in the morning. Is it your testimony that throughout that whole day until 18.00 you heard nothing about this attack that had commenced some 13 hours prior to that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not receive information about any kind of attack on Stari Vitez while I was in Busovaca. As far as the beginning of the artillery fire goes, I maintain that the artillery that I commanded did not open artillery fire at all on Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You said that. You said that you didn't know that there was an attack. Please continue, Mr. Kehoe. Ask your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me turn to the next exhibit, sir, which is a map with the grid references referenced in the military information summary.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Prosecution Exhibit 709.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. That's the map. Ask your question before the break, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, these two grid references that are set forth in the map reflect the two places that checkpoints were is set up by the HVO according to the military information summary. Now, General, the setting up of checkpoints in this fashion would reflect a degree of coordination and planning, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. Checkpoints were always there. As far as I can see from the map, this is a checkpoint by the church and I'll read it, it says GR 225935, and it was, for the purpose of civilians coming to the church who were there, who lived there, should know how far they can go and where they were entering territory controlled by the BH army, whereas the checkpoint at the grid reference GR 243923 was also a checkpoint on the main access from Zenica to town of Vitez, and they always were checkpoints. There was another one which doesn't seem to be introduced here. I don't know why. It was the checkpoint by the bus station, which was almost at the front line itself, up at the line itself, the front line itself controlled by the HVO. It was only in that way that we were able to warn civilians living in the region or coming to the region not to enter territory controlled by another army. But despite the checkpoints that existed, at night individuals under the effects of alcoholic beverage, would pass this line and become prisoners, taken prisoner by the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, this military information summary notes that all access into Vitez has been denied by the HVO at these two checkpoints. Was that a normal course of events for the HVO, to deny access into Vitez at these checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as the checkpoint is concerned, at GR 225935, that grid reference, that particular checkpoint was at the very front line itself. As far as the other checkpoint in the other position, they never received orders from me of that kind, that is to say, to block the area and to prevent anybody from entering the area of Vitez. So quite certainly they did not receive an assignment from me of that kind, and I hear for the first time that blocks of this type existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I can continue on this, Mr. President, or take a break. I can continue on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It depends. You know I like to take breaks when there's a coherent point that's been finished. If you have nothing further to say about that attack we can take a break, but if you have a few more questions --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What would you prefer?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'd prefer to continue on, Mr. President, just for a few more minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let me ask the interpreters to be a little bit patient, even one who doesn't seem to be in the best form today. Let's finish with the attack on Stari Vitez. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, given the fact that both these checkpoints denied access to Vitez, and as the milinfosum -- both checkpoints had mines laid across the road, and the troops had cam cream on their faces at the checkpoint, those would reflect a degree of planning and coordination to this attack, would it not?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have already stated that the control point located in the north-westerly position had mines and it was a checkpoint at the front line, that is to say, the point is GR 225935. It had mines in the area, and they were right up at the front line. They either cautioned people or sometimes prevented passage, because the mines were an obstacle themselves, and for -- the problem that was to ensure passage despite the snipers and the BH army positions. The checkpoint at GR 243923 quite possibly had mines but the assignment of the checkpoint was, and I think this is clearly defined in one of my documents, never received instructions to me linked to blocking passage, denying passage. The GR 243923 checkpoint never received orders of that kind, and so the HVO did not launch an attack. That is erroneously stated. The attack was launched by the PPN Vitezovi. The home guards who were in their trenches I'm quite certain did not advance one metre. There were 15 victims and they were killed and they were HVO victims, HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, just to define, cam cream that the milinfosum is talking about is the green and black cream that soldiers often put on their face; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The soldiers were at the control point, the checkpoint GR 225935, as well as the checkpoint at the bus-stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, General. I'm sorry. I'm just trying to get a clarification for the Judges as to what cam cream is, and cam cream is a black and green cream that soldiers put on their hands and faces to camouflage themselves; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Soldiers use that to camouflage themselves, to mask themselves. Sometimes it's their image, but with professional soldiers it should be only used to mask, to camouflage, but there were other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: General, let's stay with the first part of your answer, please. Let's not speak about looks or improvisations by soldiers. One would think that each person was looking into the mirror to see whether the green cream was nicer than the black cream. Let's be serious here and go on. Mr. Kehoe, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was it normal for the soldiers at these two checkpoints that we've been talking about, was it normal for those soldiers to be wearing cam cream on their faces?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Soldiers at the checkpoints that we're talking about, GR 225935 could have had all types of appearance, could have looked different. At the GR 243923 checkpoint I do believe that they were members of the police, and one would not expect the members of the police to have that kind of paint, but I repeat, the checkpoints are never -- did not receive extraordinary instructions from my command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm going to stay on this point but a different aspect of this attack, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I know that Judge Rodrigues wants to ask a question. I suggest that we take a 20-minute break, about 20, 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will now resume the hearing. Please be seated. Judge Rodrigues wants to ask the witness a question. Judge Rodrigues, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: General Blaskic, I would like to go back to document 708 and ask you whether I've read it correctly. I read it as follows: Darko Jelisic -- Gelic, rather, seems not only to be aware of the entire operation but also seems to be in agreement with the operation. Do you think that I've read this correctly?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not have that document and I do not recall everything that was stated in the document, that is to say, document 708 to which we are referring, but I expressed my views publicly to the government, the civilian authorities of Vitez, that we cannot undertake any operations whatever on Stari Vitez because we have to guarantee security and safety to the population in Stari Vitez. That position on my part was common knowledge to all the representatives of power and authority in Vitez. I would just like to have a look and see what Darko Gelic is says in document 708 if you want to ask any more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I don't think it's necessary to reread the document, but Darko Gelic knew about the helicopters, and when he spoke with the UNPROFOR officer -- well, perhaps you remember that conversation. From my reading, he seems that he knew that there were helicopters which had brought in some large pieces of equipment, and in the conversation with the UNPROFOR officer, he seems to be in agreement. So I merely wanted to know whether you agreed with this way of reading the document. We don't have to go back to it.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is possible that Darko Gelic told the UNPROFOR officer what he did connected with the helicopters, but Darko Gelic, as a liaison officer, did not have, as far as I remember, access to the contents of that. That is a logistical affair. If he had commented about this, he would have left an impression on the UNPROFOR officer. Helicopters began to arrive into the Lasva Valley at the beginning of August, so I'm not quite clear about how Darko Gelic was able to make comments about helicopters at all. As far as the activities are concerned, he was in Vitez at the time of the attack, when the attack took place, that is. Quite possibly he heard -- because, you know, there was sporadic operations daily. The forces of the BH army were at a distance of 15 to 20 metres. Sometimes the distance between them was a distance of 100 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Thank you, Judge Rodrigues. Mr. Kehoe, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, just to clarify the point you had with Judge Rodrigues, you noted during the course of your testimony that you objected to an attack on Stari Vitez, and your objection was in May of 1993, not in July 1993; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. At the end of May they invited me to attend a government meeting, the civilian representatives, and raised the three questions including Stari Vitez including a military solution. I publicly let it be known that I was opposed to that type of solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, what units in Central Bosnia have a multi-barrelled rocket launcher in their possession, what HVO units?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: What calibre do you have in mind for the multiple rocket --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Any calibre.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: For a time the command of the mixed artillery division had a MBRL. This was up until the 8th of January, 1993. The calibre was 122 millimetres. After that, the command of the artillery battalion had a 128-millimetre MBRL, and quite possibly some of the brigades had lower calibre multiple-barrelled rocket launchers, but I cannot tell you offhand, I haven't got the notes, but this was always at the level of the brigades and it was the artillery under the command of the commanders of the home Guards Brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, did the Viteska Brigade have a multi-barrelled rocket launcher in July of 1993?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: For a time it had an improvised MBRL, handmade. I don't know how it came into being and who masterminded it, but it was an improvised VBR, which had a far smaller range and less capability than the classical VBR. I know that this kind of device the Vitez Brigade had and it was workers from the weapons factory, whether from Novi Travnik or Vitez, that produced it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did the Vitezovi have a multi-barrelled rocket launcher?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I know, they did not have one. I do not have information, nor did I ever have information that they had one of these devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, when the milinfosum reflects that at 5.45 in the morning there have an occasional multi-barrelled rocket launcher and artillery fire, you conclude that this multi-barrelled rocket launcher came from a unit other than the Vitezovi, is that accurate? "Yes" or "No".

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I know, the Vitezovi, within their composition, did not have MBRLs. So perhaps they came from another unit, although there were improvised types of MBRLs, improvised devices used with -- electricity powered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I could then give the witness, Mr. Registrar, the two exhibits that we spoke of, Defence Exhibit 250 as well as Defence Exhibit 345. 250. Now, General, the first exhibit that we have, Defence Exhibit 250, is the Vitezovi report that we refer to frequently.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In the insertion that we have for the 18th of July, the document reflects the death of three Vitezovi soldiers, Marinko Plavcic, Miroslav Jankovic, and Ivo Babic. Now, let us move to the next document which is Defence Exhibit 345, and we will refer to the individuals that were killed. The first one killed in Vitez on the 18th is number 95, Vlado Ivankovic, which has no designation of being in the Vitezovi; number 137, Joze Andrija Krizanac; number 202, Veska Zlatko Nakic; number 302, I'm not sure if it's the first one, Zoran Sero, killed on the 18th; the next one is number 436, an individual from the regional police, Nikica Saric; the next one, 439, an individual from the Tvrtko II Brigade, Ive Zoran Dzandara; the next death is on 444, Roko Vukovic, also from Tvrtko; the next three dead are from the Vitezovi, and they are 446, 455, and 470, which reflect the three Vitezovi names that are in 250. Now, this document, General, reflects that there were deaths of members of the Vitezovi, during this attack, Tvrtko, the regional police, and the Viteska Brigade. So there are at least four different units involved in this offensive; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The document about the death that we mentioned a moment ago speaks of the units where these individuals who lost their lives came from. I did not find in the document the locality of their death, but I know, according to the information that I later gathered, that between 13 and 15 members lost their lives in an operation of this kind belonging to the HVO, that one of the mines fell directly on the defence positions of the HVO, and everybody in that position was killed. These were perhaps six or seven members. In this document, the list of casualties, that is, document 345, I was able to find the date, but I was not able to find the place of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the document speaks for itself. The document itself, which is a Defence Exhibit, notes the place of death, and on all those dates, it notes that it is, in fact, Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, more than the Vitezovi were involved in this, isn't that correct, "Yes" or "No," more units?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not have data of that kind, that is to say, that more units took part in that attack. I do have information that the commander of the attack was the commander of the special purposes units, Mr. Darko Kraljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sorry, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I apologise. Mr. President, I have an objection to a previous question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You can exercise your right to redirect at the proper time. This is the kind of information that you can challenge when you redirect, Mr. Nobilo. The witness is alone ordinarily. Let me remind you of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. But when, in the question, an incorrect piece of information is given, and then the witness is not a professional individual to be able to think of all this at the same time, it's not the place -- the document does not speak about the place of death but the place in which they were buried.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, he is the one who chose to be a witness. It's true he's not a witness like all the other witnesses, but I have to maintain balance. Having said that, you will have enough time to clarify all of this. Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In this attack on the 18th, there was an artillery barrage that began at 4.45 in the morning using artillery and multi-barrelled rocket launchers, checkpoints were set up, several units were involved, and your liaison officer was the spokesperson about this attack to the British battalion. This would appear to be a highly organised attack that you maintain you knew nothing about; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: First of all, as regards the artillery barrage, I continue to maintain that the artillery under my command did not function, and possibly there was an exchange of gunfire, but the artillery that I commanded quite certainly did not operate. Second, the checkpoints were always at the same points, but one of them is not included in your exhibit, and probably they tried to prevent access or leaving the area, but I was not informed of the attack and I did not receive information about the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, let us move to two more exhibits which will be a milinfosum of the 19th and the 20th of July.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Prosecution Exhibit 710.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, I also have the other one. We're going to do them together, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Prosecution Exhibit 711.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The first is a military information summary, Exhibit 710, from the 19th of July, 1993, just the area of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You will see in this document, Mr. President, Your Honours, that the military information summary is talking about a conversation with Sefkija Djidic, commander of Stara Bila town defence, and I think that the record reflects to date that Mr. Djidic was the commander of Stari Vitez. I don't think there's much question about that in the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will read this just briefly: "Vitez: 2. An attempt by the BritBat area LO to negotiate a cease-fire to stop the HVO attack on Stara Bila," it should be Stari Vitez, "was successful and came into effect on the 19th 10.30. It will end on the 20th at 22.00. 3. A conversation with Sefkija Djidic commander Stara Bila town defence, revealed the following unsubstantiated information regarding yesterday's HVO attack on the Muslim sector: a. The HVO attack began on the 18th at 04.00 and petered out at approximately on the 18th at 16.00. During this period, approximately 300 impacts (mainly rifle grenades and 60/82/120 millimetre mortars) were made in the Muslim sector. b. During the period approximately 100 HVO infantry troops attempted to attack from all directions surrounding the enclave but were unsuccessful and no ground was gained. The HVO sustained at least 6 dead, 3 of whom they claim were HV. The remaining HVO injured personnel were extracted during their own arrangements last night. The BiH claim that during the past 2 days they have sustained 20 casualties, one of whom has died. 8 of these casualties were extracted by ICRC, call sign, with BritBat, call sign, to Zenica hospital. Comment. Whether the HVO will attack Stari Vitez again is difficult to assess after this initial failure. Significantly, despite their successful defence the morale of the BiH in the pocket is reported as being low. The large expenditure of ammunition by the HVO in the context of the overall situation (cut-off) suggests that they possess large stockpiles. Comment ends." On the 20th, Exhibit 711, top of the page, and this is the military information summary of 20 July, 1993: "1. The cease-fire brokered yesterday was broken by both factions in the town earlier this morning. At the last count, 7 impacts were made in Muslim Stara Bila and five impacts in the Croat sector resulting in at least one death. 2. Darko Gelic, the 3 Ops Zone HVO LO claimed that if the BiH attack Vitez then the HVO will retaliate by shelling Zenica. He claimed further that 90 per cent of those casualties sustained by the HVO in Central Bosnia since the beginning of the conflict had been the result of fighting with the BiH." Now, General, Darko Gelic, as your liaison officer, told a liaison officer for the British Battalion that if the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina attacked Vitez, then the HVO would retaliate by shelling Zenica. Did you authorise him to make that statement to the British Battalion, General?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: First of all, I already said that Darko Gelic was a communications officer. He never received such authorisation from me, but I wish to say that the HVO of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia was attacked by the BH army, but it never shelled Zenica or any town, and that was a clear position. In any negotiations, never did I start speaking that way. I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: General Blaskic, that was not the question. The question was whether you had authorised Darko Gelic to make that statement. I suppose that you're answering "No"?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, and it's the first time I've ever heard of it. Today is the first time I've ever heard of it, and he never informed me of having presented such a position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I think that's an answer to the question. All right. Mr. Kehoe, you have an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, with regard to this attack itself, you responded, during your direct examination, that this attack without your authorisation on Stari Vitez was a gross violation of discipline and perhaps even a criminal act. What type of criminal act were you contemplating that this was?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Arbitrariness of a commander and acting in contrast to my orders. He did not inform me and he did not seek my approval, but no one from the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina or from the monitoring mission ever talked to me until I came to this court, and nobody ever told me that there was a war crime. The only piece of news was that this was a major victory on the part of the BH army and a terrible disaster and defeat for the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, again referring to your order 361 which you said applied to Kraljevic and his units, did you order, again in your paragraph 3 of Exhibit 361, that: "Individuals and groups who are completely out of control are to be arrested immediately and warrants to be delivered to the commander of the military police." Did you order that these people who violated your orders and conducted this attack be arrested and that warrants be delivered to the military police? Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As concerns what these people did, I informed the chief of the main staff about that, because not in a single point in time was I in charge of taking disciplinary or any other action against the PPN Vitezovi. As regards this extraordinary incident, I told the chief of the main staff of the HVO about everything I thought about this, also that I thought that this was a major infraction of discipline on the part of the commander of the PPN Vitezovi.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, given the fact that you thought this was perhaps a war crime, did you refer this to the military district prosecutor so that he may investigate further and conduct an investigation to see if there were crimes involved?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said that I thought that this was a criminal offence. As regards this being a war crime, that's what I heard about here in the courtroom. I thought that this was a violation, and I informed about this the chief of the main staff of the HVO, Brigadier Milivoj Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you or did you not refer this matter to the military district prosecutor for his investigation? "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The district military prosecutor? No, I did not refer this matter to him. I referred it to my superior who was in charge of taking further action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And once again during your Operation Pauk matter, nobody was ever arrested, or convicted, or disciplined as a result of this gross violation of discipline or possible criminal conduct, were they?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That unit was disbanded totally, among other things, because of these measures, and it was reorganised into a different unit but not all of the members of this unit. This was before Operation Pauk. It ceased to function as a unit on the 15th of January, 1994. In addition --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, General. That's not my question. I'll read you my question again. Regarding the Pauk matter, nobody was ever arrested, or convicted, or disciplined as a result of this gross violation of discipline or possible criminal conduct, were they? "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In Operation Pauk there was a different mandate. It did not deal with violations of military discipline, it dealt with matters related to criminal offences and with the extended mandate with war crimes too. Military discipline was -- action related to military discipline was not taken within the Pauk operation at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, let's move ahead. After you received this information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I'll ask the operation that -- the expression -- that you say operation Spider, "araignee" in French. I'm not supposed to know what the word "Pauk" is. Mr. Kehoe doesn't say operation "araignee," but he says "Pauk." I want to hear in French, "araignee," Operation Spider. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I can say the word "Spider" too, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, before you did your Grbavica attack in September of 1993, did you find out the names of the soldiers in the Vitezovi who were responsible for this gross act of insubordination that took place on the 18th of July?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, as concerns the 18th of July, the commander himself said that this was an action he had carried out at his own initiative with his soldiers. So the commander said this clearly, and we can see this from document 250, that he commanded that action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. That was Darko Kraljevic?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This person, Darko Kraljevic, who committed this act of insubordination, was the same person who selected the soldiers for you in the Vitezovi that took place -- that conducted the Grbavica attack in September; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. No, that is not right. These persons were chosen by Mr. Dragan Vinac and he subscribed to their behaviour and everything else. He was the deputy of Darko Kraljevic, and he was in charge of that particular activity. I think that he is the signatory of this document 252.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So there were Vitezovi involved in -- we're moving to the Grbavica attack that you yourself planned. There were members of the Vitezovi involved, and you don't know whether or not those members of the Vitezovi that were involved in the Grbavica attack were involved in Ahmici, or the truck bomb, or the Stari Vitez attack on the 18th of July; isn't at that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not have any knowledge of the Vitezovi taking part in Ahmici, except for information concerning certain individuals that I heard here in this courtroom. However, the unit of Vitezovi had no business there, nor did they receive orders to be there, including the village of Ahmici.
