I reacted at that time, it was a complete, full meeting, and I once again issued strict warnings that acts of that kind were prohibited, and Grubesic attended that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you discipline Grubesic as the commander of these two soldiers who took these individuals out to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I did not at the time because the statement that I received and the investigation told me that this group had stormed the prison forcibly and taken out -- this group had stormed the prison, they were not following orders, and had taken out the prisoners. So they stormed the prison, took away a certain number of detainees and took them out to do labour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, let us stay with these two individuals who stormed the prison and took these people out. What happened to them? Were they convicted? What sentence did they receive?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know that they were prosecuted at the military district court, but I had no insight as to the punitive policy of the military district court. So I don't know what punishment they received and what the decision made by the president of the military district court was. This was not my area of competence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you ensure, General, that those two soldiers were immediately removed from the HVO pursuant to the rules on military discipline?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: If they did commit a crime, and they did, then they were arrested immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's not my question, General. My question for you, as the commander of Central Bosnia, was: Did you ensure that these two people, these two HVO soldiers were removed from the HVO military ranks; "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can only answer in the following way: The commander of the brigade has the same powers as I do, and he is the individual who sorted those affairs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: General, please focus on all of the answers that you are giving to the Judges. This is a question of methodology. I think three years ago we read the famous decree about the disciplinary powers and the powers of military justice; do you remember that? I think it was Article 29; do you remember that? Do you remember the degree? It was an important decree which dealt with the organisation of military justice and so forth; do you remember? That included disciplinary powers. Please focus on the question that the Prosecutor is asking. The Judges would like to know. Because the other day you said that you couldn't take any disciplinary sanctions when the perpetrators were not identified. Do you remember that? You said that you had to wait for an investigation, that you were not competent for that investigation, and that the tribunal was competent, that is, the prosecutor, but it was self-evident that if the perpetrators were identified, then you would have disciplinary powers. Let me bring you back into a certain logical way of thinking relating to the entire answer. In this case, there were identified perpetrators. They were identified; is that not correct, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, they were, Mr. President, according to the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Therefore, you had all of those powers. Focus on the answer. Did you or did you not issue sanctions? I don't think that the question calls for long comments. Think about it, and if necessary, consult your notes. If you need to take a little time, do so. Could you give us an answer?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I personally asked for an investigation to be conducted into this particular case, and I was informed that the military district prosecutor had taken over the case and the prosecution. I personally did not issue disciplinary measures towards those perpetrators of the crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, please go back to your question because I don't think that our concerns were really addressed. You have to provide the evidence, Mr. Kehoe. We are here to listen and to get an idea of what's happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, the question is very simple and it is this, sir: Did you ensure that these two HVO soldiers were removed from the HVO? Did you do that? The answer is "Yes" or "No."

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: What I did was that a criminal prosecution was unleashed, and they were placed in the military district prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So the answer to the question is that you did not take any steps by yourself through the military disciplinary function to remove these soldiers from the HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Military disciplinary function, no, because that same measure was taken by means of the criminal prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, General. I have to tell you that I no longer understand. It seems to me that we're going round and round. If there are two soldiers who you are convinced committed the crime, it seems to me that the question is very simple. As the commander with disciplinary powers, did you take measures? I thought that you had said that you sent them to a military prison after an investigation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, at the time when the military district prosecution launched an investigation, they were placed in the military district court for investigation and they were no longer members of the HVO at that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You've just said that you asked that an investigation be carried out. I have the impression now that there are a great many investigations. You just said that you asked for an investigation. Who was doing the investigation? You? The prosecutor? Who? I don't understand. Help us.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not conduct the investigation. The investigation was conducted by the military district prosecutor from the military district court of Travnik and the assistant for security, that is to say, together. They cooperated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, were they convicted, these two individuals?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know that they were taken to the district military court, but I don't know what the outcome was, what the final decision and ruling of the district military court was. I believe that these two persons were convicted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If you believe that they were convicted, what kind of sentence did they receive?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know. What kind of a sentence do you mean? I mean, they spent time in the military prison. What else? Or perhaps they had their sentences suspended. I don't know. I was not in charge of this. I did not have any insight into the sentencing policies of the district military court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, if they had their sentences suspended, were they taken back into the HVO and into the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: My position was the following: It was quite clear to all the commanders, that is to say, that all persons who were perpetrators of criminal offences should be taken over by the department of defence and that they should get work duty, and these were general rules issued to all the commanders, that is to say, that all persons who are perpetrators of criminal offences should be assigned to work duty by the department of defence, not military duty. So in line with these instructions, these persons had to be assigned to work units with work duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But you don't know one way or the other what happened to these guys, do you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe that they were taken away after having served their sentence, and I believe that they were never mobilised by the defence department as military duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us talk about trench digging and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: General, just a moment, please. When you say, "I believe," are you telling us today that you believe or were you concerned about that at the time?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not have specific data here, but I know that they are orders that I issued, and they are here also at the Tribunal, that is to say, about sending persons who committed criminal offences from the HVO units. So this was standing practice, and it was quite clear to all commanders that these persons, weapons had to be taken away from them and that they should be sent to the defence department where they would be issued a reassignment. I do not have any information of their return to HVO units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, let me read to you part of an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm referring, Mr. President, to Exhibit 514. It's in English, so I can just read a portion of that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is an ECMM report of the 6th of February, 1993. The report is dated the 6th of February, and it notes, General, that: "There was a significant increase in the amount of digging in by HVO forces mainly using Muslim labour, some of whom had been forcibly abducted from their homes." The chairman of the Busovaca joint commission notes that he observed the use of Muslim labour to dig HVO trenches, and this is in the Busovaca area. In Exhibit 677, Prosecutor's 677, which is a military information summary dated the 6th of February, 1993, in the area designated "Busovaca," the British Battalion writes: "At Podjele, a 50 to 60-metre trench system was sighted at grid," I believe, "325898 with approximately 15 to 20 civilians digging and three HVO soldiers looking on." Moving down at Katici, and giving the grid reference, there were again reported to be civilians digging positions on the eastern edge of the village under the supervision of HVO soldiers. "Comment. These positions were in clear view of BiH positions; however, the BiH soldiers did not engage the civilians and the HVO soldiers. This leads us to believe that the civilians may have been Muslims under HVO guard. Comment ends." Let me turn to another British Battalion milinfosum, which is a new exhibit, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Prosecution Exhibit 714.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have a few for the booths so it might be a little easier, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, go ahead, please. At the end of this trial you're going to be in great physical shape.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, Exhibit 714 is another military information summary of the 7th of February, 1993, this by the Cheshire Regiment. I'm interested in the bottom of that page, talking of comments of the BiH commander. It notes: "The commander stated the following: The HVO has been using Muslim civilians to dig in the HVO offensive positions in the areas of the villages of Solakovici." It notes it's: "(Believed to be in the control of the BiH?)" "Kula, Skradno, and Podjele." Moving down to the -- skipping a paragraph, final report from Zenica, dated 7 February, 1993, stated that: "Once again, the HVO had broken the agreed cease-fire. These included the following: "A. HVO snipers in the village of Podjele," grid reference, "Bakije," grid reference, "were reported to be engaging the Muslim villages of Putis," grid reference, "and Merdani," grid reference. "The arrested Muslim civilians in Podjele have been forced to dig trenches for the HVO. "B. HVO snipers were also reported to have been shooting at civilian vehicles travelling on the Kacuni-Lugovi." "Comment: Many of the statements made by the two BiH commanders have some credence, especially with respect to the accusation of Muslim civilians being forced to dig HVO positions. However, it must be remembered that it is only giving one side of the story and the HVO made many accusations against the Muslims also breaking the cease-fire." Now, General, you would agree, would you not, that the use of Muslims and forcing Muslims to dig trenches in the Busovaca area in late January and early February 1993 was widespread, was it not?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The only thing I can say is that during that period I was isolated in Kiseljak, and during that time in Kiseljak, where I had insight, not a single Bosniak Muslim was detained or was digging trenches in Kiseljak where I was. As for the area of Busovaca, the only insight I had was the information I received from my immediate subordinates or at the meetings that were held in Busovaca, the meetings of the joint commission on the 5th of February, for example. This commander, Dzemo Merdan was commenting on this and making assertions, and I asked him to be specific in terms of these claims that Bosniak Muslims were being used for digging trenches. Whenever I received any information, I would check it out and I would prohibit that kind of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, let me read you some other testimony of an HVO soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I need, Mr. President, to briefly go into private session, because this was a closed session testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. What's going to be read by the Prosecutor was covered by protective measures. The Prosecutor is going to read a short passage, and we're going to move into a private session before we go back into public session. I'm saying this so that everybody is informed. Mr. Registrar, we're going to move into private session now. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. We're moving back into public session. Now, ask your questions. And I'm saying this for the witness and the Prosecutor, be careful not to mention the name of that individual who testified. Be careful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Because you're asking questions about the trenches. All right. Ask your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, your testimony is that your chief of staff, or no one in your headquarters, or none of your brigade commanders either in Vitez or in Busovaca, none of those individuals told you about these large number of Bosnian Muslim detainees who were taken and forced to dig trenches, is that your testimony? You knew nothing about this; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I've already said that I received this information from the International Red Cross, from Mrs. Iris, and as regards this unfortunate incident of the 7th of February, I received information about that only on the 12th and I did not receive any information about that because I was isolated in Kiseljak and I was cut off from any possible communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, let's move ahead to the period of time on the 16th and thereafter, and I'll try to move through this quickly, General. Now, on the 16th of April, on page 18577, you told us that, on line 14, that Petkovic told you that, "We should undertake the engineering type of fortifications." That means that Petkovic is telling you to dig trenches; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Undertake the building of shelters and also adjusting them for combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you noted to us that on the same day, and this is on page 18590, on line 19, "I also, at 19.45, talked to Pasko and asked him to start digging in and develop the defence further." Now, Pasko Ljubicic's subordinate was Vlado Santic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. And this digging meant that soldiers who were at the front line were supposed to dig their own shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On the 16 the of April, what role did Vlado Santic have? What position within the military police?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was commander of security. His role in the military police was commander of the first active company of the military police, although he changed roles. But specifically I do not know from which time until which time he was at which post.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On the 16th of April, 1993, he had an office in your headquarters in the Hotel Vitez, did he not, and I'm referring, of course, to Vlado Santic?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He had an office before that too. His office was at the Hotel Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, when you gave this order to Pasko Ljubicic, which I take it you would assume would be passed down the line, this order to start digging in, did you admonish Pasko that his troops should not use civilian labour or detainees to dig those trenches? Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This was always readily understood. This is something related to prisoners of war that was prohibited by law, and in 1992 I issued an order to have the territory set up, and it was readily understood this would be done by the soldiers and possibly by work units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, knowing that civilians had been taken out to dig trenches during February, with that knowledge in your mind, did you or did you not specifically tell Pasko, "Do not use civilians to dig trenches." Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I've already said that at the first meeting on the 4th of March, I made it known to all persons present there that prisoners of war could not be used for digging trenches, and this was a clear instruction on my part. As for this specific action, no, I didn't tell Pasko that because I thought that this was a lawful action, well-known to all or, rather, it was unlawful to engage prisoners of war in trench digging.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's move ahead then and talk a little bit about the testimony of Sulejman Kavazovic. Sulejman Kavazovic was one of the Bosnian Muslim men arrested in Vitez and taken to dig trenches. He was originally detained at the SDK building. How far is the SDK building, by the way, from your headquarters, do you know? In downtown Vitez?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know how far away it is. Perhaps if you show me a photograph I may remember but I can't remember where the SDK building is at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Shed some light on this SDK, what is that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: SDK was another government building in downtown Vitez approximately 100 to 150 metres from the Hotel Vitez, maybe a little bit more, where there were Bosnian Muslim detainees kept where they were taken out to dig trenches. I refer Your Honour to the testimony of Sulejman Kavazovic who testified --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Excuse me for interrupting. I made you lose some time. There is a witness and you're going to read the relevant excerpts from that testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me read you a bit of Mr. Kavazovic's testimony, General, starting at page 2321 at line 22: "Q. How long did you remain at the SDK building until you left? A I remained there 3 days. From the 19th until the 22nd I was at the SDK until I was sent to dig trenches." At line 4: "A In Vitez and all the camps that were there, some of the military policemen and even members of the HVO, they would come into the camps with vans and they would select the people that were supposed to go out and dig trenches. That day when they took me away, this same colleague of mine came along with Zabac, a military policeman, who said he needed nine people to go to Rijeka to dig trenches." On page 2326, on line 4, and he talks about going to the Bungalow: "Q When arrived at that location ...", Referring to the Bungalow, "... tell the court who you saw and what you saw. A We got out of the van. There was a restaurant there and a terrace in front of it, a concrete terrace with steps leading to it. On the terrace I saw Vlado Santic, who told me, as soon as I got out of the van, he said, 'It's you again.' Next to him I saw 13 Jokeri standing there, fighters belonging to the Jokeri unit formation." 2327, line 1: "A After that, on the orders of Vlado Santic, he ordered five Jokers, he said, "You, you, you, and you," and Zabac and those two policemen from the van, they took us to Kratine." He notes on page 2329 that he took him to Kratine, to Miroslav Bralo, Cicko. Line 19 of that page he says: "A I remained in Kratine from the 22nd until the 28th or 29th, seven or eight days. I cannot remember. Our stay in Kratine was strenuous. We had to dig dugouts where they could not dig. We were exposed to fire, HVO fire, even army fire too, because at that part where dugouts were supposed to be dug, where they as soldiers could not dig, we had to dig them all day, and we would clear the forest for them. So when they could not go through the forest we would have to cut it for them. We carried timber boards. It this was heavy physical labour. We dug trenches. We carried out their orders." This on page -- I can move ahead. We can move quickly. In conclusion, on page 2347: "Q When you arrived at the SDK building, what did you see? A When I got to the SDK building, the people whom I had left behind were there, and then I met with people who had also been digging trenches like me. So we talked to each other, where we had been, where we had done the digging, and I was waiting for the exchange. Q Where were the people you talked to say they had been digging trenches? A During the conversation we had and judging from the people who came to Kratine, I learned that people had been digging trenches at Krcevine, Dubravica, Sivrino Selo. From all the camps in Vitez people were rounded up and taken to dig trenches." Now, General, Mr. Kavazovic testifies to the ordering of his forced trench digging by a member of the military police, Vlado Santic, who had an office down the hall from yours in the Hotel Vitez. Did you know that Mr. Santic was participating in these forced -- in this forced trench digging with the military police and other HVO soldiers or were you ignorant of that as well?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I heard the testimony here for the first time before this Court. I did not receive any information related to these activities, and the orders that I issued made the opposite behaviour necessary, and these activities are in complete contrast to that. I'm talking about 116, 162,2, 364,2, 365,1, 370,9, 376,1, 373, and 378, all of this evidence shows that I took measures and I prohibited such action. When I would receive such information, I would react to this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, let us just shift subjects for a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I ask, Mr. Registrar, if the witness can be given Defence Exhibit 298 with Defence Exhibit 314, shown together, and also shown together Defence Exhibit 301 together with Defence Exhibit 325.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, does this first pair of documents, 298 and 314, reflect your order and response from Dusko Grubesic? Taking them singly, 298 is your order of 17 April, 1993 with a number of 014393/93, and in number 4 of that order, you say: "To dig in on the front lines and prepare a counterattack." The response comes back referring to your order, and that's in Defence 314, and Dusko Grubesic says in point 4: "Entrenchment has been carried out on all defence lines in order to organise the defence from the enemy as efficiently as possible." Now, General, this order that goes to, among other units, the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade, you have included no admonition in this order against using civilians to dig trenches, have you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said a moment ago, I mentioned numerous documents a moment ago which spoke about the prohibition of using prisoners of war for trench digging, whereas order 298 -- may I have a look at it, please, just have a few minutes to peruse it? Order 298 refers to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, General. I'll ask the question. Referring to Exhibit 298, knowing that members of the Busovaca brigade had forced Bosnian Muslims detainees to dig trenches, you did not include any admonition in that order to prevent such a thing from happening again; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have already enumerated all the orders that were issued concerning the treatment of prisoners of war. This particular order, order 298, has its specific topics that it deals with. In Busovaca, everything had already been done. Busovaca was in combat since January 1993. The trenches had not been filled in, and they had nothing to do --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, General. The answer to the question is, no, you did not include that admonition; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In this order, this order did not admonition, but I quoted the documents that referred to the behaviour towards prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, take a look at Defence Exhibit 301 and 325, 301 being your order to dig trenches to the Viteska Brigade and 325 a response back from the Viteska Brigade. Again, General, in this series of documents, you order in 301, in point 3, you tell the Viteska Brigade to carry out engineering works, and in Exhibit 325, the Viteska Brigade responds back that "new trenches and reinforcements are continuously being created on all defence lines." Again, General, despite the fact that you knew that HVO troops had forced Bosnian Muslims to dig trenches, you did not include any admonition in that document either; "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Just let me have a look at the documents, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I see you've finished the document, or have you not? I'll let you finish the document, General.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not yet. Just one more minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Document 301, in point 3, talks about the first degree of engineering work which implies that the soldier should dig his own shelter within 60 minutes --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. My time is very short. My question to you was --

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know, but it was not ordered here. This was not an order to dig communicating trenches, bunkers, trenches, and so on. This document limits what engineering work is to be done, that is to say, a soldier's shelter which he uses for standing up, and it takes him 30 minutes to one hour. I'm quoting from point 3 which limits the level of engineering work to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, in fact, you did tell us that on the 16th of April, 1993, and this is at page 18591: "A At 19.50, I had another conversation with the commander of the Viteska Brigade, and I asked that he start fortifying himself and get ready for a shift of positions."

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Just tell me what time, please.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is true. But it says to order, that the commander of the brigade, Cerkez, order his soldiers to dig in, that is to say, to order his soldiers to dig in, fortify.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, let me move to the testimony of one of your officers, Ivica Zeco, who, on page 11717, noted at line 7, concerning the ratio of BiH soldiers to HVO soldiers, in response to a question by

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: "Q So if we could simplify the proportion, it would be ten to one in favour of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? A Yes." Now, General, given your testimony that the ABiH attacked the HVO and given your need to dig defensive positions and that you told us that you didn't have enough time to defend the pocket, enough men to defend the pocket, who was digging your trenches? Who did you believe was digging this extensive trenching system around the pocket?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm going to try and explain. If you're asking me about shelters, then this can be seen from my order of the 16th of April at 19.50 where I ordered that soldiers of the Vitez Brigade dig shelters, whereas as far as the shelters go that are not on the front line, then this was done predominantly by the work platoons or units, that is to say, shelters, approaches. But in front of those shelters were trenches from which soldiers were defending their positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think that we should look at the interpretation for a moment because we had the same word used for "zaklon" and "skloniste," that is to say, shelter, whereas they are two words, at least in Croatian, which have different meanings. "Zaklon" is where the soldier stands up at the front line and shoots, whereas the shelter is towards the rear. I think that we ought to make a distinction here in English and try to have two different terms for the two words used; otherwise, there will be confusion. So shelter is in the rear and zaklon is up at the front line like a trench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I'm not very competent when it comes to settling that issue. Mr. Prosecutor, try to find two different terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I don't even know how it came up, to be honest with you, at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I thought that you were not aware that you were missing information. Obviously, in this area, Serbo-Croatian is a richer language than English. Let's try to translate the nuance. Mr. Nobilo, there is a difference between a shelter -- well, you really have to explain. A shelter ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: It's not just a nuance: I was in the army, it was a long time ago, but I remember that my back hurt, because in the space of 60 minutes, we had to dig out a hole in frozen ground where I would stand as a soldier with my rifle. So the zaklon is the hole in which a soldier stands to shoot, whereas a shelter is behind, is a safe place where I can rest, eat, sleep, and so on. Between this front post and the shelter behind, there are communicating trenches that have been dug in, communicating trenches between the front hole where the soldier is standing and shooting and the back shelter where he eats, sleeps, and rests. So these are different terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: If there's an offensive shelter from which one fires, then there's a refuge where, between shooting, people could take shelter. I hope your back doesn't hurt now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: That's right. They are two different terms, two different levels of digging, but essential for safety purposes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Perhaps dugout.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you for explaining that nuance to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'll go back to the initial premise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, you said you were attacked on the 16th, that you were surprised, that you had a ten-to-one ratio of soldiers against you, that you didn't have enough people to defend the pocket. On the front lines, who did you think was digging these trenches for the HVO on the front lines?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not have the document with me, but I think it was document 301, and from that document, we can see that orders are being issued for the digging of these trenches, and they don't even have to be dug out often. But natural facilities are used for protection purposes, everything that is not open space and can be used as protection. But over a longer period of time, whenever the soldiers are not shooting, they use a pick and axe to dig and fortify the terrain. In a later period, once this first attack was repelled and once we had established our positions, we mobilised work platoons --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, General. I'm sorry. Who was digging the trenches on the front lines? Given that this was a surprise attack, given that you said you didn't have enough people and were down ten to one, who was digging these trenches on the front lines?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At that time, nobody dug them, but natural shelters were used for the protection of soldiers until this order of mine. Everybody fended for themselves. They made due with what they had, the natural barriers. Sometimes it was a house, sometimes it was a ditch, sometimes it was a tree trunk, or anything of that kind. But once I issued the order at 19.50 on the 16th of April to the commander of the Vitez Brigade, it was clear that I told him in precise terms to order his soldiers to dig in, because night was coming upon them, there would be a lull in the fighting, and these soldiers could make use of this time to fortify. To the best of my knowledge, the soldiers dug these fortifications for themselves, and this is seen in document 301, where I issue orders to soldiers to affect digging on a first level, that is to say, this trench which is dug out in the space of one hour, and that is standard practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, you told us yesterday about Bosnian Muslim men coming and going from the cinema. Were they being taken to dig trenches on the front lines?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have already said, and we heard from the testimony, that there were individual cases where people were taken out to the front lines for fortification purposes, but I profoundly believe that these cases were for the purposes of shelters, digging shelters. But I did not receive information. I always said that when I heard of this, I reacted to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you, in fact, did hear that soldiers were bringing prisoners, detainees, from the cinema to the front lines to dig trenches or to dig fortifications. You did hear that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not receive reports of that kind. I received reports in May from the International Red Cross officials that work platoons were being taken to dig trenches at the Busovaca positions, and this was on the 9th of May, I think, when an official, Clare Podbielski of the International Red Cross, informed me about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, let me understand you, that you gave an order to dig trenches on the 16th of April. The Viteska Brigade reacts to that order and takes Bosnian Muslim civilians from the cinema up to dig trenches, but you don't know this is going on when it's happening, is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know -- first of all, I issued an order, and this can clearly be seen here, at 19.50 on the 16th of April, that the commander should order his soldiers to entrench. That is a precise order on the 16th of April at 19.50. I do not know that instead of ordering his soldiers, he took the civilians from the cinema and took him to do this. I have no information of that kind, nor did I ever receive information of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can continue on. I don't know if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. Go on for a few more minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, did you visit the front lines?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I visited practically all the front lines at different periods of time, and I spent a long time at the front lines in different periods, as I say. At some points, depending on where the focus of our defence was, I would spend 15 or 20 days at some positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: For instance, did you visit the front lines at Bobasi in September 1993?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would have to have a look, because you're asking me for a concrete date and a concrete time. So I would have to take a look at my chronology to see what I was doing in September, whether I visited them in September, because we lost one of these lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We're going to stop at this point and that will allow, General Blaskic, who must be tired, to look at his chronology. We will resume tomorrow morning at 10.00. Is that correct, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Court stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
